newsitem.title: USA: U.S. experts unimpressed by Thai rescue package.
newsitem.headline: U.S. experts unimpressed by Thai rescue package.

text.p: The $16 billion rescue package pledged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and a group of Asian countries may not be enough to bail Thailand out of its economic crisis, U.S. emerging market experts warned.

The package, unveiled in Tokyo on Monday, was but a modest first step toward restoring confidence in Thailand's shaky financial system, they said. And they said Tuesday's comments on the package by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers did little to calm jitters, given the absence of a unilateral aid pledge by the United States.

The IMF estimated the devaluation in July had left Thailand with a financing gap of $14 billion, and an effective rescue package should be much larger, said Thomas Trebat, head of emerging markets research at Citicorp Securities.
"In a crisis, the size of funding needs is unknowable," he said, noting that in a worst case scenario, foreigners would begin expatriating capital and set in motion a massive capital flight.
Trebat suggested that only a rescue package of "overkill" proportions could confer credibility.
Mexico's peso crisis in 1995, for example, was contained by a $43 billion bail-out from the U.S., even though only a small amount was used, he said.
By comparison, the $4 billion each pledged by Japan and the IMF to Thailand seemed paltry, Trebat said.

Confidence in Thailand among international investors was currently fragile, he said, adding that investors were in for a rude awakening after listening to a chorus of promises of "Asian economic miracles" for a decade.
Moreover, the much-touted "early warning" system to alert investors after the Mexican peso crisis obviously failed to work, he added.
Feroz Talyarkhan, a managing director at Bear Stearns and Co Inc, agreed that investors had not fully come to grips with the volatility expected in Thailand in the weeks ahead.
"We do not think the markets are prepared for the potential impact of austerity (of the IMF package) on corporate defaults," he said.

Talyarkhan, however, believed that Japan would dole out more aid because Thailand's special place in Japan's overall Asia investment strategy was comparable to that of Mexico for the U.S. and Central European countries for Germany.
"If push comes to shove, Japan would loosen the purse strings," he said.
China also indicated that it probably would contribute to help Thailand.
A U.S. fund manager said the $16 billion was "not a whole lot" considering Thailand's commitment in forward contracts.

"Enough is when you don't use all of it," he said, adding that the remarks by Deputy Secretary Lawrence Summers on the Thai currency crisis, sounded "rather empty," given the absence of a unilateral aid pledge by the U.S.
The U.S. participates in the Thai rescue package only indirectly, through its IMF contribution.

Gregory Fager, head of the Asia division of the Institute of International Finance, said the rescue package bought Thailand precious time to tackle its problems. But he added that the Thai government must still convince the international investment community it has the resolve to follow through on the tough measures and make the system more transparent.
